title: Agent loops die silently when .goose-task.md is deleted by a rebase onto main
description: ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED BY TIMELINE. Untracking .goose-task.md (necessary - it held a sudo password, ob-3i5) means any device node that merges or rebases onto main has the file DELETED from its working tree. goose-loop.sh passes it unconditionally as 'goose run -i $TASK' with no existence check, so goose fails every iteration while the loop keeps spinning on its 20s sleep and 'git commit' finds nothing to commit - no error surfaces anywhere except the untracked local log. Timeline: 03:12 UTC the file was untracked on the feature branch; 09:33 that landed on main via PR #9; 14:38 the j2 node rebased onto main; 14:38-14:48 j2 pushed 5 commits from its already-loaded session; 14:48 last commit, then silence. j2 is the only node that has rebased onto main and it is the only node whose branch no longer tracks the file. FIX APPLIED: committed docs/agent-task.template.md (credential-free, placeholders __BRANCH__/__HOST__/__DEVICE__/__BINARY__/__RESULT_NAME__) and an ensure_task() self-heal in goose-loop.sh that regenerates the task from the template when missing, substituting per-node values from ORION_DEVICE/ORION_BINARY/ORION_RESULT_NAME env vars. Verified end-to-end with a stub goose: loop detects the missing file, logs '[self-heal: ... regenerating from template]', writes a 63-line task with zero unsubstituted placeholders, and invokes goose successfully. OPERATOR ACTION STILL NEEDED: the fix only helps once a node has the new goose-loop.sh, so each stalled node must be restarted by hand (git pull, set ORION_* in the shell profile, relaunch the tmux loop). Nodes j2 (2h44m idle), r5 (9h11m), t3 and t4 (15h25m) are all currently not producing work.
close_reason: Fix landed in a6d22c7 on main: ensure_task() self-heal in goose-loop.sh regenerates task from template when .goose-task.md is missing. Verified present in current branch after rebase.

title: Run the device-fleet bandwidth-scaling study (Pi 5 / RK3588 / Jetson Nano)
description:
THE FIRST REAL MEASUREMENTS, and the strongest result available without the O6. See ADR 0005.

Run bench_gdn on all three devices at 30 repeats and collect CSV plus a manifest per device. Use the core-tuned binaries: bench_gdn_pi5_a76, bench_gdn_rk3588_a76 (taskset to the big cluster), bench_gdn_rk3588_a55 (little cluster), bench_gdn_jetson_a57.

The study, not the individual numbers, is the deliverable. The three devices span 17 / 25.6 / ~34 GB/s of spec bandwidth. If GDN decode is bandwidth-bound at ~0.25 FLOP/byte as METRICS.md argues, achieved throughput should track spec bandwidth roughly linearly and INDEPENDENTLY OF CORE GENERATION.

The discriminating case: the Pi 5 has the NEWEST cores (A76, Armv8.2, dotprod) but the LOWEST bandwidth (17 GB/s, 32-bit LPDDR4X), while the Jetson Nano has the OLDEST cores (A57, Armv8.0, no dotprod) and MORE bandwidth (25.6 GB/s, 64-bit LPDDR4). If the Nano beats the Pi 5 on the scan kernel despite three ISA generations less capability, that is strong evidence for bandwidth-boundedness rather than a confirmation-biased result.

Also: extrapolate to the O6's 100 GB/s and publish it as a PREDICTION, so it can be checked later if a board arrives. Predicting then confirming is far stronger than measuring once.

Verify achieved GiB/s against each device's spec sheet - the RK3588 figure is estimated from its quad-channel 16-bit interface and needs confirming on hardware. Do not close this bead without committed manifests (PLAN.md section 9).
close_reason: Fleet bandwidth-scaling study landed via the cherry-pick of bench/j2's analysis: results/figures/fleet_bandwidth_scaling.md plus bench/fleet_analysis.py as the regenerator, and FINDINGS 5b. The discriminating test from ADR 0005 is answered: the Pi 5 beats the Jetson on all three kernels despite 33% LESS spec bandwidth, so the pure bandwidth-bound thesis is INCOMPLETE at seq=64 - at 4096 channels the working set is ~1 MiB and L2/L3-resident, making it instruction-overhead-bound rather than DRAM-bound. Core microarchitecture dominates. Follow-on ob-bf7 covers the replicate-spread problem that prevents any quantitative slope; the O6 prediction ships as ~3-8 GiB/s rather than a fitted line.

title: Standalone GDN kernel microbenchmark for any aarch64 device (Armv8 upward)
description:
Bridges verified-correct to MEASURED. The maintainer has Armv8 devices available, which unblocks real Arm silicon numbers without the O6.

Build a dependency-free, statically-linked aarch64 binary that can be copied to any Armv8+ device and run to produce the project's first real performance numbers. Must: time all three GDN kernels (cumdecay, gated scan, causal dwconv1d) at Qwen3.5-4B shapes (2048 channels, chunk 64) and 0.8B shapes; report which dispatch path actually compiled in (SVE/NEON/scalar); follow docs/METRICS.md's statistical protocol (discarded warmups, N repeats, p50 and p95, never a single best run); emit CSV rows conforming to docs/RESULTS_SCHEMA.md; and derive achieved memory bandwidth so the bandwidth-bound thesis can be checked against the device's spec rather than asserted.

Armv8 caveats to respect and report rather than paper over: most Armv8 cores have NO SVE (so this measures the NEON path, which is the point), i8mm needs Armv8.6+, and dotprod needs Armv8.2+. The binary should report what it actually detected.
close_reason:
bench_gdn.c plus scripts/build_device_bench.sh. Dependency-free, statically-linked microbenchmark: one binary copies to any aarch64 device and runs with no toolchain, Python, or shared libs on target. Four ISA variants built (armv8a / armv8.2dot / armv8.6i8mm / armv9sve2). Times all three kernels at verified Qwen3.5-4B and 0.8B shapes, follows METRICS.md protocol (3 discarded warmups, p50/p95, refuses N<5), reports the dispatch path actually compiled in (verified: armv9sve2 reports sve, armv8a reports neon, so dispatch is real not collapsed), emits schema-conforming CSV, and derives achieved GiB/s from explicit traffic accounting so the bandwidth-bound thesis can be tested against device spec rather than assumed.

Documented loudly in docs/FINDINGS.md section 5 that QEMU timings are performance-MEANINGLESS (emulation artefacts, up to 97% spread) and must never appear in a result table - QEMU's role here is correctness only. No performance results are claimed yet; the apparatus is ready and awaits real silicon.

title: Author minimal per-operator ONNX probe graphs for the NOE op-coverage audit
description:
Prep work that makes ob-t3b.1 mechanical the moment the NOE SDK is in hand: emit one minimal ONNX graph per GDN constituent operator family so a cixbuild failure is attributable to exactly one operator.

Deliberately hand-authored with onnx.helper rather than exported from torch. The torch exporter fuses and decomposes ops unpredictably, so a rejected torch-exported graph would not tell us WHICH operator the compiler choked on - which is the entire point of the audit. Hand-building also avoids a ~300MB torch dependency for graphs that are a few KB each.

Probe families, mirroring Qwen3.5's verified GDN layer shapes (linear_conv_kernel_dim=4, linear_key/value_head_dim=128, linear_num_key_heads=16):
  1. causal depthwise Conv1D with left padding
  2. gated decay as Log -> CumSum -> Exp (ONNX has no CumProd op, so this decomposition is itself a coverage question)
  3. delta-rule state update (MatMul / outer product / Sub / Transpose)
  4. elementwise gate chains (Sigmoid / Softplus / Mul)
  5. ONNX Scan and Loop control flow - the chunkwise recurrence needs one of these, and NPU compilers frequently lack control-flow support. This is the most likely failure point and therefore the most valuable probe.

Done when the generator runs, every graph passes onnx.checker, and a README documents the exact cixbuild invocation to run against each once the SDK lands.
close_reason: scripts/npu_op_probe.py emits 6 minimal per-operator ONNX graphs into artifacts/npu_op_probe/ with a manifest. Hand-authored via onnx.helper rather than torch-exported so a cixbuild failure is attributable to exactly one operator. Verified known-good before use: all 6 pass onnx.checker full_check, all 6 execute under onnxruntime 1.28 with finite outputs, and the causal conv is verified genuinely causal (perturbing the last timestep leaves earlier outputs bit-identical). README documents the cixbuild invocation and how to record results, including the silent-CPU-fallback case which looks like success and performs like failure.

title: NOE op-coverage audit for GDN operators on an x86 host (no board required)
description:
Unblocked by the 2026-08-02 CIX finding (docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md 2.2a): the NOE Compiler is a direct download with no approval gate, requires Python 3.10, and runs on an x86 Linux HOST rather than the board. So the highest-value early finding in the whole project is available today with no hardware.

Install the SDK in a miniforge Python 3.10 venv, verify with 'cixbuild -v', then attempt to compile the GDN constituent operators and record exactly what the compiler accepts, silently falls back on, or rejects: causal Conv1D, cumulative-product/decay gating, the delta-rule state update, and the elementwise gate chains. Export minimal ONNX graphs for each op rather than the whole model so failures are attributable to a single operator.

This directly addresses risk R3 and produces docs/FINDINGS.md content that is reusable by anyone porting a GDN-class model to this silicon. A negative result ('the NOE Compiler has no kernel for a gated recurrent scan') is the finding, not a failure - it is the empirical justification for routing the scan to GPU/CPU in the mapping ADR.

Only RUNNING the compiled artifact needs the board; compiling does not. Supersedes the hardware-gated framing of ob-8xc for the compile-time half of that audit.
notes: Dependency on ob-37v (arch audit) removed as over-specified: the probe graphs only needed the GDN layer SHAPES, which were already verified from primary sources in docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md 2.3 (conv kernel 4, key/value head dim 128, 16 key heads). A full per-checkpoint architecture audit was not a prerequisite for operator coverage. ob-37v remains valuable for the mapping work but does not gate this.
close_reason: AUDIT COMPLETE on x86 host with no board. Headline: every arithmetic operator GDN needs is natively supported (CumSum -> ArmCumulate, delta rule -> ArmMatMul/ArmEltwise, causal conv -> ArmDepthwiseConv), but the sequential recurrence is NOT expressible - Scan rejected outright, Loop accepted only with a compile-time-constant trip count via silent static unrolling (no loop survives in the IR), Loop with runtime trip count rejected ('Graph is not DAG'). Empirically confirms the CPU-first mapping: keeping the scan on CPU is not a preference, the NPU has no construct for it. Also surfaced two undocumented environment facts (cixbuilder wheel is cp310-only; cixparse imports tensorflow even for ONNX). Written up in docs/FINDINGS.md 1 with logs committed under artifacts/npu_op_probe/audit/. Caveat: frontend lowering only - per-op NPU-vs-CPU placement and throughput still need full cixbuild and on-device runs (ob-8xc).

title: Define benchmark metrics precisely
description: Pin down decode tokens/sec, prefill throughput, time-to-first-token, peak memory (split into weights, KV cache, and recurrent state), and energy per token, including exactly where each timer starts and stops. Ambiguous metric definitions are how benchmark comparisons quietly become meaningless.
notes: PLAN.md leaves two things unspecified that this bead must pin down (flagged during ob-q35): (1) the minimum repeat count N for a reportable figure, and (2) which percentiles are mandatory (p50/p95/p99?). CONTRIBUTING.md deliberately describes these qualitatively rather than inventing numbers.
close_reason:
docs/METRICS.md written - operational definitions for the whole frozen metric vocabulary, such that two people measuring independently get comparable numbers.

Load-bearing timer decisions: t_submit (prompt handed to an already-warm model) is the shared origin, so model load and JIT are never inside any metric; TTFT INCLUDES tokenization since the schema calls it user-facing, while prefill_tokens_per_sec EXCLUDES it (forward-pass invocation to last-position logits) so the two answer different questions; token 1 belongs to PREFILL not decode, since it comes from the prefill pass's own last-position logits, making decode's numerator N-1 over a single wall-clock span rather than a mean of per-step rates.

Statistical defaults: 3 discarded warmups; 30 repeats for headline numbers at 4K/32K, 10 minimum at 128K/262K, never below 5; p50 and p95 mandatory with p99 explicitly NOT mandated because at N=10-30 a p99 is indistinguishable from reporting the max, which the project prohibits; two configs differ only if |delta p50| exceeds 2x the larger spread AND their p50-p95 ranges do not overlap.

Memory is never derived from RSS (which cannot separate the three components) but from model introspection plus config-derived formulas.

Corrected after the fact: the agent was launched before ADR 0003 fixed the state size, so it used 262,144 elements/layer. Patched to the 4B's 524,288 (96 MiB/token across 24 GDN layers, ceiling ~993 tok/s from state traffic). Its central conclusion survived unchanged - arithmetic intensity is 0.25 FLOP/byte for BOTH checkpoints, because MACs and bytes both scale with state size, which makes the bandwidth-bound argument a structural property of the rank-1 update rather than an artefact of one model's dimensions.

title: Quantization policy with FP16 carve-outs
description: Decide per-layer INT8/INT4 assignment and which tensors must stay FP16. Recurrent state and gating signals are the prime suspects for precision sensitivity: unlike a KV cache, GDN state is fed back through every step, so quantization error accumulates over the sequence rather than staying local.
notes: ELEVATED to P0 2026-08-02. The decode traffic breakdown (docs/METRICS.md appendix) shows weight streaming is ~95-99% of decode bandwidth, so weight quantization - not kernel work, not state narrowing - is the dominant decode-throughput lever: INT4 weights take the 4B from ~12.5 to ~50 tok/s at 100GB/s. This is now the highest-value optimization decision in the project, and it is where KleidiAI's INT4/i8mm GEMV micro-kernels (109 of them A720-usable) apply directly.

title: INT8 KV cache quantization: shifts the GDN O(1) vs full-attention O(n) crossover
description:
The context-length scaling results (§17, ob-mrd.10) show full-attention decode degrades 1.55-2.1× from ctx=1→4096 while GDN stays flat. INT8 KV cache quantization halves the KV cache memory traffic, directly extending this story: it shows how much the crossover point moves when full attention is quantized, and whether GDN's architectural advantage persists even against a quantized baseline.

Implement INT8 KV cache in the e2e decode loop (gdn_e2e_decode.c):
- Store K and V as int8_t with per-head float scale (group-wise quantization)
- NEON dequantize-on-the-fly in the attention score and value-gather loops
- Add --kv-int8 compile flag alongside the existing --int8-weights flag
- Benchmark the full ctx-sweep grid: FP32/INT8-weights × FP32/INT8-KV across ctx lengths
- Document in FINDINGS.md §20 with the updated crossover analysis

This is the natural next optimization after INT8 weight quantization (ob-8qt.11). Both the GEMV weight path and the KV cache path are bandwidth-bound; quantizing both shows the combined effect on decode throughput and the net architectural comparison.
close_reason: Landed in 43a3dbd. INT8 KV cache quantization implemented with NEON dequantize-on-the-fly. All 4 quant configs benchmarked on 0.8B + 4B models. 1.7-2.6× full-attn speedup at ctx=4096, 1.8× combined INT8 speedup, 4× KV memory reduction. FINDINGS §20, results/figures/kv_int8_scaling.md.

Currently the full-attention path uses simulated identity attention with a single-token KV cache — the scaling behavior is completely missing. title: INT8 weight-only quantization for CPU decode GEMV — 2-4× bandwidth reduction
description: Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: FP32 GEMV achieves 54-57% of LPDDR4x peak. Weight-only INT8 quantization cuts weight memory traffic 4x (FP32→INT8+scale), directly improving tok/s. Approach: per-output-column INT8 weights with FP32 scale, dequantize-on-the-fly in NEON inner loop. Cortex-A76 has dotprod/i8mm so SDOT is available for INT8×INT8 path if needed. Implement behind -DINT8_WEIGHTS compile flag, benchmark both FP32 and INT8, report tok/s delta. Natural follow-up to ob-8qt.9 GEMV row-sweep optimization.

title: Fleet data: run-to-run spread exceeds cross-device effects; needs one commit-matched sweep
description: The fleet bandwidth-scaling data cannot currently support any quantitative scaling slope, because same-code variance is larger than the cross-device differences being interpreted. Evidence from the committed CSVs plus manifest git SHAs: (1) rk3588-t3 and rk3588-t4 are the SAME source commit 28729f3 on the same core class and differ 1.68x on gdn_gated_scan 4B seq=64 (1.96 vs 3.29 GiB/s) - same code, so this is environment: different physical boards, cluster pinning, governor, or thermal state, none of it recorded. (2) pi5-r5 and pi5-j1 are the SAME physical board (identical hostname r5 and 'Raspberry Pi 5 Model B Rev 1.0') at different commits and differ 1.53x (1.20 vs 1.84); that may be a real optimization gain but nothing separates it from the t3/t4-scale variance. (3) No commit-matched run covers the Jetson AND an A76 device, so even the headline Jetson-vs-Pi5 comparison is cross-commit - it survives only because the effect is large relative to the spread. WHAT SURVIVES: the qualitative result that the Pi 5 beats the Jetson on all three kernels despite 33% less spec bandwidth, so the pure bandwidth-bound thesis is incomplete at seq=64 working sets (~1 MiB, L2/L3-resident, so instruction-overhead-bound). WHAT WAS WITHDRAWN: per-device '% of spec' figures and an A76-pair fit of 1.79x-throughput-for-2.00x-bandwidth that I had added to FINDINGS.md - it mixed f127a11 Pi5 data with 28729f3 RK3588 data, and choosing the other same-commit RK3588 host gives 1.63x instead of 2.74x from identical hardware. FIX: one sweep across every device at a single pinned commit, with taskset pinning, governor, and pre/post thermals recorded per run, then recompute. title: Verified-correct SVE2 reference kernels for decay, scan, and causal conv1d
description:
DONE 2026-08-02 - fp32 reference implementations of all three primitives KleidiAI lacks, cross-compiled for aarch64 and numerically verified under QEMU with no board.

Key insight: vectorize across the CHANNEL axis and walk the sequence with a scalar loop, so no cross-lane prefix-scan network is ever needed. Qwen3.5-4B's 2048 linear-layer channels give far more parallelism than a 4-lane vector absorbs.

Verified bit-identical to an independent precision-matched scalar reference for the scan and conv history; conv output differs by one fp32 ULP from svmla FMA contraction. Causality exact (zero leak). Predicated tails exercised at 2051 channels. Vector-length-agnostic (identical at 256-bit). Scalar fallback bit-identical.

NOT verified: performance. QEMU says nothing about A720 cycles, cache, or bandwidth.

Follow-on work is tracked separately: i8mm/dotprod delta-rule matmuls via KleidiAI (ob-8qt.2), a bf16/fp16 state variant to halve state traffic, and on-device performance measurement.
notes:
SVE1 vs SVE2 question resolved: the kernels were already SVE1-clean (every intrinsic is base SVE, guard is __ARM_FEATURE_SVE), verified identical on SVE1 at 128/256/512-bit incl. neoverse-v1 and a64fx, on SVE2, and on no-SVE. File renamed gdn_sve2.c -> gdn_sve.c since the old name overstated the requirement. Consequence: Graviton3 (SVE1-only) works, so ADR 0002's hedge fallback is safe.

The variant that WAS missing is NEON: GCC 13 -O3 emitted ZERO NEON ops for all three kernels on -march=armv8-a (the inner loop's serial dependency blocks vectorization and GCC will not interchange loops to vectorize across channels). Added explicit NEON paths with vfmaq_f32 and a scalar tail; inner loop now compiles to fmla v1.4s and results match the SVE path. This matters because Apple silicon has NO SVE and most deployed Armv8 Android devices do not either. Dispatch ladder is now SVE -> NEON -> scalar, all three verified to agree.

title: Measure engine-boundary crossing cost (16 crossings per token in a 3:1 hybrid)
description:
The cost the CPU-first mapping hypothesis must answer, and a publishable result in its own right - no per-crossing figure appears to have been reported for the CIX P1.

A 3:1 hybrid alternates 3 GDN -> 1 attention eight times, so a CPU/accelerator split crosses the engine boundary 16 times per token (8 out, 8 back). Payload is small (~5KB FP16 at the 4B checkpoint's hidden_size=2560), so the cost is INVOCATION LATENCY, not bandwidth.

Measure, per engine (NPU via NOE, GPU via Vulkan/OpenCL): round-trip dispatch latency for a trivial kernel on a ~5KB tensor, with and without zero-copy/shared-memory buffers; then the same at prefill-sized payloads. Report distribution, not a best case.

The decision this feeds: if single-dispatch latency exceeds the single-token attention matmul it replaces, decode should keep attention on CPU/GPU and the NPU earns its place in prefill only - the phase-dependent mapping in PLAN.md 3.1. Do not assume the answer; the whole point is to measure it.

title: Hand-written SVE2/i8mm chunkwise gated delta-rule scan for Cortex-A720
description:
THE CENTREPIECE under the CPU-first mapping hypothesis (PLAN.md 3.1). Implement GDN's chunkwise recurrence directly against Armv9.2: SVE2 predicated vector ops for the elementwise gate and decay chains, i8mm/SDOT for the delta-rule matmuls where precision allows, FP16 kept for the recurrent state per the quantization policy.

Why the CPU rather than an accelerator: the chunk-to-chunk dependency is sequential and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, which is exactly what a low-latency OoO core handles well and a wide parallel engine handles badly; and the recurrent state stays resident, avoiding a per-token cross-engine transfer through 24 GDN layers.

Why this is the right thing for THIS competition: Cortex-A720 is Arm IP, so this is Arm-architecture optimization rather than tuning a third party's NPU - which is what the 40-point Arm-specific criterion rewards.

Structure the kernel so the chunk-parallel inner math and the sequential outer scan are separable, since the mapping ADR may later move the inner math to GPU/NPU while the scan stays on CPU.

Portable across any Armv9 SVE2 device, so it is also runnable on the Edge AI hedge target - this bead is the reason the core contribution survives the board not arriving.
notes:
Toolchain settled (docs/FINDINGS.md 3): build with clang>=17 or gcc>=13 using -mcpu=cortex-a720, which enables Armv9.2-A + SVE2 + i8mm (both NEON smmla and SVE svmmla) + BF16 + dotprod. Verified via predefined feature macros with a +sme control.

CRITICAL DESIGN CONSTRAINT: SVE2 on Cortex-A720 is 128-bit - same width as NEON. SVE2 buys PREDICATION (whilelt for clean chunk tails, no scalar epilogue) and gather/scatter, NOT more lanes. Do not frame any result as a vector-width win.

Cortex-A720 has NO SME/SME2, confirmed from LLVM's AArch64Processors.td and feature macros.

KleidiAI (HEAD 98872b0) coverage: 109 of 185 matmul micro-kernels are A720-usable (neon/dotprod/i8mm) and DO cover the delta-rule matmuls - reuse them rather than reimplementing. But all 4 dwconv kernels are SME2-only, so KleidiAI gives us NOTHING for the causal depthwise Conv1D on this core, and it has no cumsum/prefix-product/scan primitive of any kind (verified by repo-wide search).

So this bead's novel content is exactly three kernels: causal depthwise Conv1D for SVE2/NEON, gated cumulative decay with predicated tails, and the chunkwise gated delta-rule scan. Shape them like KleidiAI micro-kernels so they are upstreamable - that is the Potential Impact argument.
Fp32 reference implementations of all three primitives are DONE and verified (see the sibling bead and docs/FINDINGS.md section 4). This bead now covers the optimization work on top: i8mm/dotprod integration for the delta-rule matmuls, a bf16/fp16 state variant (halves state traffic, the dominant GDN decode cost), big.LITTLE placement, and on-device tuning. Also note GCC 13 rejects -mcpu=cortex-a720 (added in GCC 14) - use -march=armv9.2-a+sve2+i8mm+bf16 on GCC 13, or clang >= 17.
big.LITTLE affinity study COMPLETE. 5-config sweep on RK3588 A76/A55 at M={1,64} x K=128 x N={128,2048}. Key finding: Linux EAS places M=1 decode on little cores without pinning - 7.3x penalty. Big-core pinning REQUIRED for decode. SVE2 path cross-compiled for cortex-a720: 126 SVE instructions verified (ld1w/st1w/fmla predicated, incw/incd VL-agnostic). FINDINGS sec 23. Commits c371bb5, 2a040c8. Remaining: bf16/fp16 state variant needs A720 hw (RK3588 has no bf16).

title: Characterize the chunkwise WY recurrent-scan bottleneck
description: Determine whether GDN cost is dominated by the inherently sequential state update or by the chunk-parallel matmul portion, and how that balance shifts between prefill and decode. This is the crux: a sequential scan and a dense matmul want completely different engines, and the answer dictates the mapping decision.
close_reason: Characterized via FLOP analysis + kernel microbenchmarks + per-layer profiling on RK3588-t4. Key finding: sequential GDN kernels (gated_scan + cumdecay + conv1d) account for only 2.69% of per-layer FLOPs. Matmul portions (input projections 41%, FFN 46%, output projection 10%) dominate at 97.31%. Ratio is phase-independent (same at prefill seq=64 and decode seq=1). Sequential scan costs ~5 µs/token at decode on A76 — negligible vs ~47ms per-layer decode. The recurrence matters for pipeline depth (loop-carried dependency) and toolchain incompatibility (NPU can't express runtime-length recurrence), NOT for compute cost. Mapping implication: optimize matmuls, leave sequential scan on CPU. FINDINGS.md updated (commit 078fa4b).

title: DECISION/ADR: layer-to-engine assignment across NPU, GPU, and CPU
description:
Fix the partitioning with measurements behind it. WORKING HYPOTHESIS as of 2026-08-02 (PLAN.md 3.1), to be confirmed or refuted rather than assumed: Armv9.2 CPU hosts the 24 GDN linear layers (sequential scan, bandwidth-bound at decode, recurrent state stays resident), while the 8 full-attention layers and dense FFN blocks go to GPU and/or NPU (large dense matmuls).

Note this is the reverse of the naive 'offload everything to the NPU' framing, and it is deliberate: on the CIX P1 the Cortex-A720/A520 cores and the Immortalis G720 GPU are both Arm IP while the NPU is the only non-Arm engine, so CPU+GPU work is what the competition's 40-point Arm-specific optimization criterion actually rewards.

Must account for boundary-crossing cost (bead ob-t3b.3): 16 crossings per token in a 3:1 stack, latency-dominated rather than bandwidth-dominated. Expect the outcome to be a PHASE-DEPENDENT mapping - NPU earning its place in prefill where matmuls amortize dispatch, decode possibly staying entirely on CPU/GPU - rather than one static assignment. Record whichever way the measurements fall.

1. Auto-detect clusters by max frequency (group CPUs by cpuinfo_max_freq)
2. Set performance governor (sudo, record before/after state)
3. Capture thermal baseline (all thermal zones)
4. Report memory info (free, meminfo, DMC frequency if available)
5. Enumerate available governors and current OPPs
6. Generate ready-to-paste taskset commands for each cluster
7. Output structured JSON alongside human-readable text

This is portable: the script is written and tested on the RK3588 (2-cluster) today, and will work on the O6 (3-cluster) on arrival with no changes.

title: Document decode-phase narrow-format penalty in FINDINGS.md
description: The refreshed 28-row CSV reveals that at decode (seq=1), bf16/fp16 gated_scan variants are ~2x slower than fp32 (4.52/5.63 vs 9.27 GiB/s). At prefill (seq=64), narrow formats help because I/O savings dominate. At decode, the data is L1/L2 cache-resident (~80 KiB), so conversion overhead (fp32↔half) dominates over I/O savings. This means state narrowing is a PREFILL optimization, not a decode one — the opposite of the naive assumption. Document this in FINDINGS.md under the mixed-precision section.

title: Software prefetch hints for NEON inner loops
description: Add __builtin_prefetch calls inside the NEON time-step loops to prefetch data 2 steps ahead, hiding the ~10-cycle L2 latency. The gated_scan kernel is at 1.1% of compute peak (latency-bound), so this has potential. The conv is compute-bound (less likely to benefit). Apply to NEON paths of all fp32 kernels first; extend to mixed-precision if effective.
close_reason: Negative result: software prefetching made all kernels 8-26% SLOWER on the A57. The hardware prefetcher already handles GDN's strided access pattern (stride = channels*4 bytes). The extra PRFM instructions are pure overhead. Reverted all prefetch code. Lesson: on Cortex-A57, do NOT add software prefetch hints for sequential/strided streaming patterns.

title: Conv kernel double-width NEON unrolling
description: Apply the same double-width unrolling technique (8 channels/iter, 2 NEON register groups) to the causal dwconv1d kernel. The conv has a 4-deep FMA dependency chain per iteration (acc=h0*w0 + h1*w1 + h2*w2 + cur*w3), so it benefits even more from ILP than gated_scan/cumdecay (which have only 1 FMA/iter). With single-width, the 4-cycle A57 FMA latency creates stalls in the chain. With double-width, the 2 independent chains can be interleaved by the out-of-order scheduler.
close_reason: Landed in e244a7e. Conv double-width NEON unrolling: 1.5× on 4B, 1.6× on 0.8B. Cumulative conv speedup from baseline: 3.3×.

title: NEON double-width unrolling for gated_scan kernel (8 lanes/iter)
description:
The gated_scan kernel processes 4 channels per NEON iteration (128-bit). The A57 has 32 NEON registers and the kernel body uses only 3-4. Processing 8 channels per iteration (2 NEON register groups) doubles work per branch and gives the OoO engine more independent instructions to schedule.

Implementation: unroll the NEON channel loop by 2 (process vi*8 and vi*8+4 in the same iteration). Only for gated_scan and cumdecay (the highest-traffic kernels). Scalar tail and SVE paths unchanged.

Acceptance: gated_scan shows 10-20% additional improvement on top of OpenMP. Tests still pass.
close_reason: Landed in 71ccc23. 1.52-1.75× additional speedup from 8-lane NEON unrolling. Combined with OpenMP: cumdecay 4.11×, gated_scan 3.95× vs serial. Tests bit-identical.

title: OpenMP multi-threaded parallelization of GDN kernel channel loops
description:
All three GDN kernel families (cumdecay, gated_scan, causal_dwconv1d) and their fp16/bf16 variants iterate over channels independently — the channel loop is embarrassingly parallel. On the Jetson Nano A57 (4 cores) we are leaving 3x throughput on the table.

Add '#pragma omp parallel for' to the channel loop in each kernel, guarded by '#ifdef _OPENMP'. Build with -fopenmp. This is portable C that benefits every multi-core device in the fleet (Pi5, RK3588, Jetson, Graviton, O6).

Acceptance criteria:
- All kernels parallelized with OpenMP pragma on the outer channel loop
- Build succeeds with and without -fopenmp (graceful fallback to serial)
- Correctness tests still pass (no race conditions — channels are independent)
- Benchmark shows ≥2x speedup on 4-core A57
acceptance_criteria: All 11 kernel variants build with -fopenmp; tests pass; benchmark shows ≥2x speedup on 4-core A57

title: Cheap check: does the RK3588 NPU toolchain also reject a runtime-length recurrence?
description:
A one-day generalisation check on the project's headline finding, made possible by the RK3588 having its own ~6 TOPS NPU (Rockchip RKNN).

We established that the CIX NOE Compiler cannot express a runtime-length sequential recurrence: Scan rejected, Loop only via static unrolling, Loop with runtime trip count rejected (docs/FINDINGS.md section 1). If RKNN - an entirely independent vendor toolchain - fails the same way, the finding stops being 'a CIX limitation' and becomes 'edge NPU toolchains generally cannot host a linear-attention recurrence'. That is a much stronger and more reusable claim, and it directly strengthens the Potential Impact argument.

Method is already built: feed the SAME seven ONNX probe graphs in artifacts/npu_op_probe/ to the RKNN toolkit and record what it accepts, silently falls back on, or rejects. The probes are hand-authored and pre-verified under onnxruntime, so a rejection is attributable to the toolchain rather than a malformed graph.

Strictly time-boxed: if RKNN setup exceeds a day, abandon and record that instead. The submission is about Arm, not Rockchip, and a negative on effort spent is not worth losing core work over.
close_reason: RKNN cross-vendor probe landed in e3e7aa6 (cherry-picked from t4's 81b54b6). Finding: RKNN accepts Scan (CIX rejects), but runtime-Loop rejected by BOTH vendors. CPU-hosts-recurrence assumption holds cross-vendor.

title: bf16/fp16 recurrent-state variant of the GDN kernels
description:
Attacks the actual GDN decode bottleneck rather than a proxy for it.

CORRECTED FIGURES 2026-08-02 (read from Qwen3.5-4B config.json, see docs/adr/0003): per-layer recurrent state is n_value_heads x d_k x d_v = 32 x 128 x 128 = 524,288 floats = 2.0MB fp32, which is 48MB across the 24 GDN layers - DOUBLE the 262,144 figure previously quoted here. That earlier number came from the GDN-2 paper's 1.3B config and happens to match Qwen3.5-0.8B (16 value heads), not the 4B. State is read AND written every token, so bf16 halves ~96MB/token of traffic to ~48MB.

Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so kernel cleverness cannot help it; narrowing the state can. This is the one lever that moves decode.

Add bf16/fp16 state variants of gdn_gated_scan and gdn_cumdecay. CRITICAL PRECISION CONSTRAINT already established: the DECAY ACCUMULATOR MUST STAY FP32 regardless - a decay of 0.5 compounded over 64 steps is ~5e-20 and underflows fp16 outright. Mixed precision (narrow state, wide accumulate), not uniform narrowing.

This is also where SVE2 finally earns its keep over SVE1: widening multiply-accumulates (svmlalb/svmlalt) and bf16 dot. The fp32 kernels needed only base SVE.

Gate on the correctness oracle with long-context runs, since recurrent-state error accumulates over the sequence rather than staying local.
notes:
RE-SCOPED 2026-08-02 after computing the decode traffic breakdown (docs/METRICS.md appendix). Earlier framing of this bead as 'the one lever that moves decode' was WRONG.

At 100GB/s the traffic split per decode token for Qwen3.5-4B is: weights 7.5GiB at fp16 or 1.9GiB at INT4, versus GDN state 96MiB fp32 across 24 layers. So state is ~5% of decode traffic at INT4 weights and ~1% at fp16. Halving it to bf16 buys ~2-3%, not a step change. The dominant decode lever is WEIGHT QUANTIZATION (INT4 takes decode from ~12.5 to ~50 tok/s by this model), which is ob-qpa/ob-onz territory and where KleidiAI's INT4/i8mm GEMV kernels matter.

Still worth doing, but as a MEMORY optimization: halving resident state (48MB -> 24MB across 24 layers) helps fit long context alongside weights. Dropped from P1 to P2 accordingly, and the precision constraint stands - the decay accumulator must remain fp32.
close_reason: Landed in b96e12a. Four mixed-precision kernel variants added (cumdecay_bf16/f16, gated_scan_bf16/f16) with fp32 accumulators. Correctness verified: bf16 state 0.38% error, fp16 state 0.05% error, cold-gate range stress confirms bf16 no-flush and fp16 expected-flush. Determinism and 2-chunk continuity tested. Benchmark shows cumdecay_f16 at 1.46 GiB/s (+34% vs fp32) on Jetson A57; gated_scan variants unchanged at seq=64 as expected (state is ~1% of traffic at prefill, benefit concentrated at decode).

title: Reuse KleidiAI i8mm/dotprod matmul micro-kernels for the delta-rule updates
description:
Do not reimplement what Arm already ships. 109 of KleidiAI's 185 matmul micro-kernels are usable on Cortex-A720 (neon/dotprod/i8mm families; the 76 SME/mopa ones are not, since A720 has no SME). These cover the delta-rule small matmuls.

Pick the right packed-GEMM variants for our shapes (key/value head dim 128, 16 key heads) and precisions, wire in KleidiAI's LHS/RHS packing functions, and benchmark against a naive intrinsics implementation to confirm the reuse actually wins at our sizes - KleidiAI is tuned for larger GEMMs and may lose on small per-chunk matmuls, which would itself be worth reporting.

Keeps the novel work in this project confined to the three primitives KleidiAI genuinely lacks (causal conv on non-SME, gated prefix product, sequential scan).
close_reason: KleidiAI packed-GEMM evaluation landed in 1940877 (cherry-picked from t3's c152007). Finding: KleidiAI matmul 1.7-3.6× faster than hand-NEON, but packing cost makes NEON faster at decode (M=1). Phase-dependent recommendation: KleidiAI for prefill, NEON for decode. FINDINGS.md §8.

title: Evaluate the Tensilica HiFi 5 DSP as a fourth compute engine
description:
The CIX P1 has a compute engine the plan has ignored entirely: a Tensilica HiFi 5 DSP, spec'd at up to 32 8-bit MACs for AI (Radxa product page, verified). Tiny next to the NPU's 28.8 TOPS, so this is NOT a throughput play and should not displace CPU/GPU/NPU work.

Why it is worth a bead at all: we already hold the DSP SDK (dsp_sdk_v0.1_20250704_02), so 'CPU + GPU + NPU + DSP' is a demonstrable four-engine heterogeneity story rather than an aspirational one, which reads well against the 25-point WOW criterion. A plausible fit is the elementwise gate chains or the causal conv, which are small and streaming-shaped.

Deliberately P3 and stretch-labelled: pursue only if the mapping ADR lands early and the core CPU/GPU path is already measured. First step is cheap - check whether the DSP SDK exposes anything usable for fp16/int8 elementwise work, and record the answer either way in docs/FINDINGS.md.
